sec.title: Background
sec.p: Pilocytic astrocytomas (PAs) are central nervous system tumors that predominantly occur during the first two decades of life and typically arise in the cerebellum, optic pathways, hypothalamus, or brainstem. Intraventricular PAs are extremely uncommon, accounting for less than 4% of all cases, and adult presentations are particularly rare. We report the first documented case of an intraventricular PA in an adult patient in Brazil and highlight its clinical and therapeutic relevance.

sec.title: Case report
sec.p: A 32-year-old Brazilian woman presented with a secondary epileptic seizure. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an expansive lesion in the left lateral ventricle. The tumor was surgically resected, and histopathological examination showed a biphasic neoplasm with eosinophilic granular bodies and microcystic areas. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated positivity for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2 (OLIG2), with no expression of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 protein (IDH1 R132H). Expression of 5’-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP), alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome X-linked (ATRX), and the tumor suppressor protein p16 (INK4a) was retained. The Ki-67 (MIB-1) proliferation index was low, at approximately 1%, consistent with a WHO Grade 1 glioma.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This case illustrates a rare intraventricular PA in an adult, confirmed through clinical, radiological, and histopathological integration. It emphasizes the importance of including PA in the differential diagnosis of intraventricular tumors in adults and may contribute to guiding recognition and management of rare ventricular tumors in this population.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Pilocytic astrocytomas (PAs) are a subtype of gliomas originating from astrocytes, a type of glial cell [1]. They are classified as Grade 1 tumors by the World Health Organization (WHO), indicating slow growth and low malignant potential [2]. Predominantly affecting children, PAs account for approximately 20% of all central nervous system (CNS) tumors in the pediatric population, making them one of the most common brain tumors in this age group [3]. However, their occurrence in adults is rare, representing only 2% of all gliomas in this population [4]. When complete surgical resection is achieved, the 10-year survival rate is approximately 95%, underscoring their favorable long-term prognosis [5].

In children, PAs are most frequently located in the infratentorial region, particularly in the cerebellum. In adults, although cerebellar involvement remains common, other frequent locations include the cerebral hemispheres (36%), optic pathways and hypothalamus (9%) - especially in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1- brainstem (9%), and spinal cord (2%) [4, 6]. The intraventricular occurrence of PAs is extremely rare, accounting for only 4% of all cases, with limited reports available in the literature [7, 8]. To our knowledge, this represents the first reported case in the Brazilian population.

Differentiating PAs from other intracranial tumors can be challenging, as several lesions may exhibit similar clinical presentations and radiological features. Accurate diagnosis requires a multidisciplinary approach, incorporating neuroimaging characteristics, patient demographics, and histopathological findings. This comprehensive evaluation is essential to distinguish PAs from other low-grade gliomas, high-grade gliomas, and non-neoplastic conditions. Among the key differential diagnoses, ependymomas and choroid plexus papillomas should be carefully considered, particularly when tumors arise in overlapping anatomical locations or present with similar imaging patterns [1–3].

Herein, we describe the first documented case of an intraventricular PA in an adult patient in Brazil and review its clinical, radiological, and pathological aspects in the context of the current literature. A 32-year-old woman presented with a secondary seizure, prompting neuroimaging evaluation. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a well-demarcated, expansile lesion located in the left lateral ventricle, warranting further diagnostic investigation.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A comprehensive literature search was conducted in the PubMed, SciELO, and LILACS databases to perform a narrative review. The search strategy employed a combination of controlled keywords, including “Pilocytic astrocytoma”, “Adult patient”, “Case report”, and “Case series”. Studies were included if they focused on intraventricular PAs in adult patients (≥ 18 years), and comprised case reports, case series, original research articles, or systematic reviews. Only studies published in English, Portuguese, or Spanish from 1990 to present. Full-text availability and the presence of clinical, radiological, or pathological data pertinent to the diagnosis or management of adult intraventricular PA were mandatory for inclusion.

Inclusion criteria comprised observational studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses reporting on clinical presentation, neuroimaging characteristics, histopathological and immunohistochemical findings, treatment modalities, and prognostic data in adult patients with intraventricular PAs. Exclusion criteria included animal or in vitro studies, articles exclusively involving pediatric populations (unless containing relevant data extrapolatable to adults), reports lacking histopathological confirmation, and non-peer-reviewed literature such as editorials, expert opinions, or letters to the editor. Duplicate articles and studies with significant methodological limitations were also excluded.

Following this review, we conducted a retrospective case analysis of a rare adult intraventricular pilocytic astrocytoma (PA) diagnosed and managed at our institution. Patient data were obtained from electronic medical records and included demographic details, clinical history, neurological examination findings, neuroimaging studies, surgical approach, histopathological analysis, postoperative course, and follow-up information. The pre-surgical evaluation involved differential diagnosis based on clinical and radiological features, initially raising suspicion for other intraventricular tumors such as ependymoma or central neurocytoma. Neuroimaging was performed using a 1.5 Tesla MRI scanner with a protocol that included T1-weighted sequences (pre- and post-gadolinium with the standard dose of 0.1mmol/kg, in accordance with institutional MRI protocols), T2-weighted, FLAIR, and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), employing a slice thickness of 5 mm and a matrix resolution of 256 × 256. This imaging approach was essential for detailed assessment of lesion characteristics, anatomical localization, contrast enhancement patterns, and mass effect.

This study was approved by the Institutional Research Ethics Committee of São Francisco University (Approval #: 77075224.7.0000.5514). Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study. Written informed consent for participation and for publication of clinical data was obtained.

sec.title: Demographic and clinical overview
sec.p: A narrative review of 51 adult patients (≥ 18 years old) diagnosed with PA was conducted, with the findings summarized in Table 1. Patient ages ranged from 18 to 75 years, with a mean age of 34.4 years. The sex distribution showed that 58.8% of the patients were male, while 41.1% were female. The most common presenting symptom was headache, followed by visual disturbances and ataxia. Additionally, four patients presented with seizures, similar to the manifestation in our case. In terms of tumor location, the lateral ventricles were the most frequently affected sites, with 31 cases (60.78%). Of these, 16 tumors were identified in the right lateral ventricle, 13 in the left lateral ventricle, and two cases had unspecified lateral ventricular involvement. The third ventricle was involved in 9 cases (17.64%), and the fourth ventricle in 11 cases (21.56%).

Reported patient ages have ranged from 18 to 75 years, with both sexes affected [6–22, 28, 38, 39]. Clinical presentations were heterogeneous, with the most common symptoms related to increased intracranial pressure, such as headache, nausea, vomiting, ataxia, and visual disturbances. Seizures were less frequently reported [6, 8, 9, 13, 19, 21]. Neuroimaging findings typically revealed T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense lesions, often with cystic components or heterogeneous enhancement [7, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 18, 28]. Tumor locations varied, including the lateral ventricles, third ventricle, fourth ventricle, and occasionally the septum pellucidum [6–9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 19, 21, 22, 28, 38]. Surgical approaches varied based on tumor location and institutional expertise, ranging from transcortical and transcallosal craniotomies to endoscopic and suboccipital methods [6–11, 13–20]. Although gross total resection was often the goal [6–8, 10, 11, 14–16, 19], several cases reported subtotal resections [9, 12, 13, 15, 21], some followed by radiotherapy or chemotherapy [10, 12, 13, 15, 20]. Postoperative outcomes were variable, with some patients experiencing full neurological recovery [6, 7, 10, 11, 14, 19], while others developed transient or persistent deficits [8, 9, 13, 15], tumor recurrence [13, 15, 20], or, in rare instances, mortality [16, 18].

Our Brazilian case presents distinct characteristics compared to previously published adult cases. The patient, a 32-year-old woman, exhibited an uncommon presentation of isolated seizure activity, without accompanying signs of intracranial hypertension or cerebellar dysfunction. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-demarcated lesion within the atrium of the left lateral ventricle, an exceptionally rare anatomical location for PAs. The lesion appeared hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with interspersed cysts and no calcifications. Surgical resection was performed via a parieto-occipital craniotomy, achieving gross total resection. Importantly, the patient demonstrated no postoperative neurological deficits and remained clinically stable. This case is notable for its combination of an unusual tumor location, atypical clinical manifestation, and favorable postoperative outcome without recurrence or the need for adjuvant therapy. It adds novel insight to the limited literature on adult intraventricular PAs and highlights the necessity of considering this diagnosis, even in atypical clinical and anatomical contexts.

These findings not only provide a structured overview of the demographic and clinical characteristics of intraventricular PA in adults but also lay the groundwork for further discussion. The identified trends and patterns are explored in greater detail in the following sections, which analyze radiological, histopathological, and therapeutic aspects.

sec.title: Clinical presentation and diagnosis
sec.p: The diagnosis of PAs in adults requires an integrated and multidisciplinary approach, combining clinical evaluation, neuroimaging, histopathological examination, immunohistochemical profiling, and molecular analysis. Although PAs are predominantly observed in pediatric populations, their occurrence in adults, especially in intraventricular locations, presents unique diagnostic challenges due to overlapping radiological and histological features with other central nervous system neoplasms [2].

Clinical manifestations of PAs vary depending on tumor location. Common symptoms include headache, secondary to increased intracranial pressure, and ataxia, particularly in cases involving the cerebellum. Additional symptoms may include seizures, behavioral changes, and visual disturbances [9]. MRI is the first-line modality for radiologic assessment. Typically, PAs appear as well-circumscribed, often cystic masses with an enhancing mural nodule. These lesions demonstrate hypointensity on T1-weighted images and hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences. Post-contrast imaging frequently reveals vivid enhancement. However, imaging features are not pathognomonic and may resemble other intraventricular tumors such as ependymomas, central neurocytomas, or choroid plexus neoplasms [11]. In selected cases, advanced modalities such as MR spectroscopy, diffusion-weighted imaging, or positron emission tomography (PET) may provide additional metabolic or cellular insights, though their use remains limited in routine diagnostics.

Histopathological analysis remains essential for definitive diagnosis. PAs are classified as WHO grade I tumors and exhibit a characteristic biphasic architecture composed of densely fibrillary areas containing Rosenthal fibers - elongated, eosinophilic structures within astrocytic processes - and loosely textured microcystic zones with eosinophilic granular bodies. Hyalinized blood vessels and low mitotic activity are also common findings, aiding in the differentiation from higher-grade gliomas [12].

Immunohistochemical profiling further supports diagnosis and enhances specificity. PAs typically express glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), S100, and OLIG2, consistent with their astrocytic origin [13]. A low proliferative index (Ki-67 < 2%) is consistent with their indolent behavior. The absence of staining for IDH1 R132H, ATRX, and p53 helps distinguish PAs from diffuse gliomas. In diagnostically challenging cases, additional markers such as epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and MAP2 may help exclude other entities, such as ependymomas [2]. Degenerative changes, including calcifications and ischemic necrosis, may occasionally be observed [12].

sec.title: Molecular pathogenesis, genetic alterations, and targeted treatment strategies
sec.p: Molecular profiling has become critical for the diagnosis, prognostication, and therapeutic stratification of PAs. The most prevalent genetic alteration is the KIAA1549::BRAF fusion, observed in over 60% of cases, especially in pediatric cerebellar tumors [26, 29]. This intrachromosomal fusion results from a tandem duplication at chromosome 7q34, creating a chimeric protein that lacks BRAF’s autoinhibitory domain. Consequently, the MAPK/ERK pathway is constitutively activated, driving tumor growth [3, 32]. This alteration is a crucial diagnostic marker and aids in differentiating PAs from diffuse gliomas, which typically harbor IDH mutations [31].

In contrast, the BRAF V600E point mutation, present in < 10% of PAs, is more frequently found in non-cerebellar and adult cases and may be associated with more aggressive clinical behavior [36] Importantly, this mutation has therapeutic implications. Tumors with BRAF V600E respond to selective BRAF inhibitors (e.g., vemurafenib, dabrafenib), whereas those harboring the KIAA1549::BRAF fusion are resistant to such agents but may benefit from MEK inhibitors like trametinib [32, 33].

Unlike diffuse astrocytomas, PAs generally lack IDH1, TP53, and ATRX mutations, reinforcing their classification as biologically distinct entities [31, 34]. Although immunohistochemistry can identify IDH1 R132H mutant protein, comprehensive mutation profiling using PCR or NGS is often necessary for definitive molecular characterization [31].

The presence of the KIAA1549::BRAF fusion is associated with a favorable prognosis and may predict responsiveness to MEK inhibition. Conversely, BRAF V600E mutations or deletions in CDKN2A may suggest a higher risk of recurrence or therapeutic resistance [36]. While most data are derived from pediatric cohorts, emerging evidence supports similar molecular patterns in adult PAs, including those in intraventricular locations.

sec.title: Treatment and prognosis
sec.p: The cornerstone of PA treatment is surgical resection. Gross total resection (GTR) is often curative, given the indolent nature of these WHO grade I tumors. Long-term outcomes are excellent following complete resection, and adjuvant therapy is generally unnecessary [3]. However, when complete resection is not feasible due to the tumor’s proximity to critical neuroanatomical structures, such as the hypothalamus or brainstem, the risk of recurrence increases, and additional treatment may be required [2]. In cases of incomplete resection, depending on the size of the residual tumor, close neurological observation with serial imaging follow-up is generally recommended. Should there be evidence of tumor progression, such as radiologic progression or worsening of the patient’s symptoms, a new surgical approach may be considered. Additionally, adjuvant therapies such as radiotherapy or chemotherapy can be employed selectively. Importantly, management and follow-up should be conducted by a multidisciplinary team including neurosurgeons, oncologists, and radiologists [2, 3].

For incompletely resected or progressive tumors, adjuvant therapies include radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Chemotherapeutic regimens, especially in pediatric populations, commonly include carboplatin and vincristine, with temozolomide or the combination of Chloroethyl-Cyclohexyl-Nitrosourea (CCNU) or lomustine, vincristine, and procarbazine used in selected cases [35, 36].

Targeted therapy is increasingly considered based on molecular profiling. BRAF V600E-mutant tumors may respond to BRAF inhibitors, whereas tumors harboring the KIAA1549::BRAF fusion exhibit resistance and are more responsive to MEK inhibitors [32, 33]. Accurate molecular diagnosis is thus critical for guiding appropriate targeted therapies.

In cases where PAs obstruct cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow and cause hydrocephalus, neurosurgical interventions such as ventriculoperitoneal shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) may be required to restore CSF circulation [1].

Overall, prognosis is generally favorable, particularly when GTR is achieved. Tumor location and molecular profile further influence outcomes. Cerebellar tumors tend to have better prognoses, while deeply located tumors may pose greater surgical challenges. Integration of surgical, histopathological, and molecular data is essential for tailoring management and improving long-term patient outcomes [3, 29, 30, 32, 33].

sec.title: Differential diagnosis of pilocytic astrocytoma
sec.p: The differential diagnosis of PAs encompasses both neoplastic and non-neoplastic intracranial lesions. Among primary brain tumors, key considerations include hemangioblastomas, metastatic lesions, and atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors, which may exhibit overlapping imaging and histopathological features. Additionally, when PAs occur within the ventricular system, the differential diagnosis must include ependymomas, choroid plexus papillomas, and meningiomas, all of which commonly arise in intraventricular locations [1].

Beyond neoplastic entities, non-neoplastic conditions such as brain abscesses and cavernomas can mimic PAs on neuroimaging, particularly when presenting with contrast-enhancing lesions or cystic components. Therefore, a comprehensive diagnostic approach, incorporating clinical evaluation, advanced neuroimaging (MRI with contrast), histopathological examination, and immunohistochemical analysis, is essential to accurately differentiate PAs from other intracranial pathologies [1, 37].

In cases where complete resection is not feasible, the management of residual disease depends on the size, location, and clinical impact of the remaining tumor. Asymptomatic remnants may be monitored through serial imaging and neurological assessment, with reoperation considered in the event of progression. Although PAs are generally indolent, adjuvant therapies such as radiotherapy or chemotherapy may be considered in selected cases of progressive or unresectable lesions. These decisions should be made within a multidisciplinary framework involving neurosurgeons, oncologists, and radiologists to optimize individualized patient care.

sec.title: Case presentation
sec.p: A 32-year-old woman was admitted to the Emergency Department at São Francisco University Hospital (HUSF), Bragança Paulista, São Paulo, Brazil, following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, her first-ever seizure episode. Her past medical history included controlled Crohn’s disease and anxiety disorder, but no prior neurological conditions. She had been breastfeeding for six months and reported allergies to latex, shrimp, and iodine. Her regular medications included adalimumab, prednisone, sertraline, and a progestin-only oral contraceptive. Upon stabilization, she was alert, lucid, and oriented to time and place, but reported a holocranial headache. Phenytoin 100 mg every 8 h was initiated for seizure control.

No specific pre-surgical interventions were undertaken aside from initiating neurophysiological monitoring and anticonvulsant therapy due to the patient’s history of seizure episodes. The differential diagnosis of the intraventricular expansive lesion, based on radiological characteristics and anatomical location, primarily included ependymomas and choroid plexus tumors, which were carefully considered during the preoperative planning. As part of the initial diagnostic workup in this emergency scenario, a non-contrast cranial computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrated a well-defined, slightly hypodense lesion measuring approximately 2.6 × 3.5 × 3.1 cm (anteroposterior × longitudinal × transverse) within the atrium of the left lateral ventricle. The lesion caused moderate dilatation of the temporal horn of the left lateral ventricle without evidence of hydrocephalus, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of choroid plexus papilloma.

Subsequent contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated an expansive lesion centered in the atrium of the left lateral ventricle, exhibiting homogeneous hypointensity on T1-weighted images, hyperintensity on FLAIR and T2-weighted sequences, and containing small internal cysts (Fig. 1). Post-contrast imaging revealed intense, heterogeneous enhancement outlining the cystic areas, alongside solid components that lacked enhancement. The lesion displayed well-defined, regular margins contiguous with the ependymal surface and was not associated with surrounding parenchymal signal abnormalities. Measuring 3.4 × 2.8 × 3.1 cm (length × anteroposterior × transverse), the lesion caused marked dilation of the atrium and temporal horn of the left lateral ventricle without evidence of cerebrospinal fluid transudation.

caption.p: Axial brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrating an intraventricular tumor located in the atrium (trigone) of the left lateral ventricle in an adult patient with a first seizure episode. The post-contrast T1-weighted image (left) reveals a well-circumscribed, heterogeneously enhancing lesion with subtle adjacent ependymal enhancement, suggesting localized involvement of the ventricular wall. The T2-weighted sequence (center) demonstrates a predominantly hyperintense lesion containing internal cystic areas, consistent with a mixed solid-cystic composition typical of low-grade gliomas. The FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery) sequence (right) shows heterogeneous signal intensity within the lesion and mild perilesional hyperintensity, indicative of gliosis or vasogenic edema. No evidence of hemorrhage, calcification, or hydrocephalus was observed. These features are consistent with a slow-growing glial neoplasm, such as pilocytic astrocytoma

sec.p: As mentioned earlier, initial cranial CT performed after the patient’s first seizure revealed a well-defined lesion consistent with the MRI findings, which provided sufficient anatomical and lesion characterization to guide surgical planning. Given the radiographic features suggestive of a low-grade glial tumor and absence of systemic symptoms, additional metabolic imaging such as positron emission tomography (PET) was not pursued; moreover, PET was unavailable at our institution. While comparative radiological analysis of other intraventricular tumors—including subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, central neurocytoma, or metastases—could offer additional context, the lesion’s imaging characteristics, location, and clinical presentation strongly favored a differential diagnosis between pilocytic astrocytoma and ependymoma.

The patient underwent a left parieto-occipital craniotomy with complete tumor resection. Intraoperatively, the lesion appeared purplish, friable, and highly vascularized with irregular blood vessels. The postoperative course was uneventful, with discharge on postoperative day five, and the patient remains under semiannual outpatient follow-up with no imaging evidence of tumor recurrence and remains disease free at 36 months.

Supratentorial ependymomas typically demonstrate a predilection for the frontal lobe and present with heterogeneous imaging characteristics, including relatively well-defined margins, significant perilesional edema, and intense, heterogeneous contrast enhancement. Signal intensities on T1- and T2-weighted sequences are usually heterogeneous within the tumor. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) often reveals restricted diffusion corresponding to high cellularity, reflected by low apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values.

In contrast, pilocytic astrocytomas (PAs) generally appear as well-circumscribed lesions, frequently with cystic components and mural nodules that enhance homogeneously. PAs tend to exhibit homogeneous hypointensity on T1, hyperintensity on T2 and FLAIR sequences, and typically lack diffusion restriction, presenting with high ADC values indicative of low cellularity. Furthermore, relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) values in PAs are usually low to mildly elevated, consistent with their benign biological behavior, whereas ependymomas often show moderate to high rCBV, reflecting greater vascularity and more aggressive features [40].

Clinically, the presentation of a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure with a well-defined lesion localized in the atrium of the lateral ventricle, lacking significant perilesional edema, aligns more closely with PA than with ependymoma, which typically presents with more extensive edema and variable clinical symptoms.

Histopathological examination revealed a biphasic glial neoplasm characterized by densely cellular areas composed of elongated glial cells with mild nuclear atypia, eosinophilic granular bodies, and scattered microcystic foci, with no mitotic activity observed (Fig. 2). Immunohistochemical analysis showed strong positivity for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) (Fig. 2) and oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2 (OLIG2), confirming glial lineage. The Ki-67 proliferative index was low (< 1%), consistent with a low-grade glioma. Absence of the IDH1 R132H mutation was confirmed by negative immunoreactivity for mutant IDH1 protein, and Tp53 expression exhibited a wild-type pattern. Preserved expression of 5′-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP), alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome X-linked (ATRX), and p16 (INK4a) indicated intact tumor suppressor pathways. Collectively, these findings support the diagnosis of pilocytic astrocytoma (PA), WHO Grade 1. Moreover, both PAs and ependymomas may exhibit strong positivity for glial markers such as GFAP and S100, complicating differential diagnosis. Ependymomas typically display membranous or dot-like staining for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), generally absent in PAs. Conversely, nuclear and cytoplasmic expression of OLIG2 is frequently observed in PAs but is usually low or absent in ependymomas. These immunohistochemical distinctions, together with histopathological features, were pivotal for establishing the definitive diagnosis. A detailed summary of the immunohistochemical profile is provided in Table 2, which highlights the expression patterns critical for the pathological classification of this tumor.

(Left) Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining at ×200 magnification shows a biphasic architecture with alternating compact piloid regions and loose, microcystic areas. Classic diagnostic features include Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies, which are strongly associated with pilocytic astrocytoma. (Right) Immunohistochemistry for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) reveals diffuse and intense cytoplasmic staining throughout the tumor, confirming its glial origin

sec.p: In the context of differential diagnoses such as ependymoma and choroid plexus papilloma, it is important to highlight their distinct immunohistochemical profiles. Unlike PAs, ependymomas typically express markers such as EMA and NHERF1/EBP50, which are useful for confirming ependymal origin and distinguishing them from other glial or metastatic neoplasms. The characteristic dot-like or ring-like staining pattern of EMA and EBP50 is highly specific for ependymoma, although sensitivity may vary depending on histological grade [41]. Choroid plexus papillomas.

(CPP), in turn, generally express EMA with a diffuse membranous pattern, and transthyretin (TTR) serves as a highly sensitive and relatively specific marker characteristic of these tumors; GFAP positivity is rarely observed [42].

Table 3 provides a comparative overview of PA, Supratentorial Ependymoma (EPN), and CPP, highlighting differences in typical anatomical location, radiological features, histopathological architecture, and immunohistochemical profile. High-Grade Astrocytoma with Piloid Features (HGAP) may enter the differential diagnosis of PA due to overlapping piloid morphology; however, HGAP exhibits high-grade characteristics, including increased mitotic activity, nuclear atypia, and frequent CDKN2A homozygous deletion, resulting in loss of the tumor suppressor protein p16 (INK4a), which impairs cell cycle regulation and contributes to the aggressive behavior of these tumors. Although molecular testing for alterations such as KIAA1549::BRAF fusion or BRAF V600E mutation could provide additional diagnostic and prognostic value, such analyses were not performed in this case. The diagnosis was based on histopathological and immunohistochemical findings, which were consistent with PA. This limitation has been acknowledged in the context of the available clinical and pathological evidence.

sec.title: Concluding remarks
sec.p: PAs are exceptionally rare in adults, particularly when located within the ventricular system. To date, no published cases of intraventricular PA in adults have been reported in South America, despite existing series describing PA in other intracranial locations. This gap may reflect both the true rarity of the condition and limitations in regional reporting or scientific dissemination. Nevertheless, PA should remain a key consideration in the differential diagnosis of adult intraventricular tumors, owing to its distinct radiological, histopathological, and molecular features.

Despite the significance of this case, certain limitations must be acknowledged. Molecular profiling, including assessment of BRAF mutations and KIAA1549::BRAF fusions, is currently not included in our institution’s routine diagnostic protocols, which restricted our ability to perform molecular analyses and limited insights into potential therapeutic targets and the tumor’s biological behavior. Additionally, although the patient remains clinically stable with no evidence of recurrence, the follow-up period is still limited, precluding definitive conclusions regarding long-term outcomes. This case highlights the importance of including PA in the differential diagnosis of intraventricular tumors in adults, especially in regions where it is rarely encountered, as its accurate recognition may guide more appropriate therapeutic decisions and improve patient outcomes, particularly in settings where high-grade gliomas are more frequently assumed.

Future research should focus on the establishment of multicenter case series and molecular studies to better define the clinical spectrum, genetic alterations, and treatment responses of adult intraventricular PAs. Such efforts are essential to improve diagnostic precision and inform evidence-based therapeutic strategies for this rare tumor subtype.
